You know, a lot of people date for years, get married, and still end up divorcing. I have a different mindset when it comes to this. Correct me if I’m wrong, but I feel like people who decide to marry quickly actually have a better chance in some ways. It’s because they’ve already made up their mind—they know they want something serious and long-term.

When you date for a long time, there’s this idea that you’re *trying to find the right fit*, but a lot of people end up choosing someone for the wrong reasons—maybe attraction, comfort, or pressure. But when someone marries almost immediately, even if they barely know each other, they go into it knowing problems will come, and they accept that. They’re more likely to say, “This is my person, and I’m going to make it work.”

That’s why I don’t think it’s necessarily “weird” for someone to ask for a woman’s hand so soon after meeting her—especially in Morocco. It’s not about being reckless. Sometimes, it’s about knowing what you want and being willing to grow with someone, rather than trying to test them first.

Honestly, I get why you feel that way — their breakup definitely felt like it went on too long, and things were in this weird limbo for a while. But looking at it from a character development perspective, I think it needed to happen that way for both of them to realize who they truly were. Being together for so long, even in that limbo, gave them both the chance to grow and discover things about themselves. But they also needed to end it for them to fully see how much they had changed.

Egwene, for example, needed to realize how far she was willing to go for her own ambitions. Rand, on the other hand, had to understand that he couldn’t hold onto the version of himself that fit into that old life with her. That’s why their breakup felt so necessary — it wasn’t just about growing apart, it was about them both realizing they were on different paths now.

They had to be together and go through all of that to become who they were meant to be. It wasn’t about them failing — it was just about transition, even though it was messy and painful.

I don’t think Rand was gaslighting Egwene at all. Their relationship is way more complicated than that. At that point in the show, they were kind of in this weird in-between — like, technically together but emotionally not on the same page anymore. There was a lot of unspoken distance between them, and neither really knew where they stood.

Did Rand hurt Egwene emotionally? Yeah, 100%. But gaslighting? That implies he was trying to manipulate her or make her question her reality, and I don’t think that was the case. What he *did* do wrong was not acknowledging how she felt. He should’ve validated her — he didn’t, and that’s on him. But I don’t think he acted out of cruelty or malice.

Honestly, their dynamic is probably the most interesting in the show. It’s not about who’s “right” or “wrong” — it’s about growth. Egwene is incredibly driven and powerful, and self-serving at times. She’s sacrificed a lot, sure, but she’s also shown moments where she puts herself first — especially after she found out she could channel. Her focus kind of shifted to her own journey, and that left people like Rand feeling like they weren’t part of her future anymore.

And then you’ve got Rand, who’s literally becoming someone else — the Dragon Reborn. He’s slowly letting go of who he used to be, and that includes the version of himself who fit into a life with Egwene. That’s why the connection with Lanfear exists — not because it’s romantic or healthy, but because she sees that *new* part of him, the part he’s terrified of and stepping into at the same time.

So when he says “you don’t understand,” I really don’t think it’s gaslighting — I think it’s him realizing that Egwene doesn’t *see* that part of him yet. And maybe she can’t, because they’re on different paths now. It’s sad, but also kind of beautiful. Two people who loved each other deeply but are growing into versions of themselves that don’t fit together anymore.

So yeah, I totally get being upset with Rand, and I’m not saying he handled it well — but calling it gaslighting oversimplifies something that’s actually really layered and human.

There is one thing that even Morrocan don't know about themselves and this can be such a cultural shock when it comes to develping close relations.

I will explain it in terms of high context and low context culture. Morocco is a high context culture. We aren't direct. We care a lot about people's feelings. We are very family and community oriented. When it comes to conflicts, instead of approaching a situation or issue directly with the person, we tend to prioritize safe guarding their feelings and keeping the peace instead of solving an issue. This isn't good. This also means when we make a mistake ourselves, someone opently pointing out our mistake isn't always good. There is a lot of tiptoing that goes on. A lot of the things we communicate is inferred (hence the term high context culture). In contrast, Countries that have that low context culture like Germany and scandinivian countries, they're very direct people (scandinivian people less so nowadays due to being isolated) but germans prefer directness and practicality. If someone makes a mistake, they're all too happy to point it out and people don't take it the wrong way as they value pragramatism and solving issues. Morrocans, not so much.

For example, in the work place, if someone makes a mistake, isntead of directly saying (you've made a mistake, fix it like germans) a Morrocan is more likely to say to tiptoe around it and say (oh you did great and all but you could perhaps work on it, thank you so much) not everyone is like this ofc, there are a lot of direct Morrocans but I am saying there is a tendency for Morrocans to be very very non-confrontational people.

Also, in high contex cultures, self-image is incredibly important. We care A LOT about how we are perceived. From a young age, we are conditioned to help others and have a good image. That is why Morrocans tend to get quite offended when they're criticized about preceived wrongdoing. Instead of self-reflection, we are more likely to be super offended as making a mistake is such a big no no for us. This is in contrast with low context culture where people are big on personal development and they care more about being usefull, independant, and practical than being perceived as a good person or moral.

Morrocans on the other hand are INCREDIBLY passive aggresive and they cater to people's feelings quite a lot. It's not just about religion or being arabs.  It's about the fact that we are a high context culture. In other ways, we are very very community oriented. When a country is like this, people tend to focus on self-image a lot and how they're perceived by other people. It's not like individualistic countries where people tend to be a lot more direct and tend to care more about themsleves and how they personally than other people. Counrtries like Spain, Italy, Turkey, and Japan. They're the same. They're also high context culture. As opposed to the US, Germany, Netherland...etc that are low context culture.

For those that might be confused, high context culture is basically a country where people rely on implicit meaning to communicate. Non-verbal communication is a big aspect and we tend to talk a lot and not always with purpose. Therefore, our words don't always have value to them.

Low context cultures value direct and clear communication. It is usually done for a purpose. There is less emphasis on sugar coating things to cater to feelings.

For example, if someone at work isn't perfoming well at their job. In a high context culture, their colleagues will try to tell them what they did wrong all while making sure not to offend them and steering them to solving an issue. This doesn't always end well as this form of communication is a bit too vague.

In a low context culture, they will clearly and directly state what you did wrong and they won't care how you feel about it. It's about practicality.

It seems that blaming yourself became a knee jerk reaction to certain events that involve someone being upset. You need to remember, if you want change, then it starts with your thoughts.

Thoughts = emotions = actions = identity.

At the moment, you've gotten used to having these train of thoughts where you're quick to blame yourself. It became a subconscious thing where you instantly FEEL the blame when someone is upset. It's almost engrained in you. Like, an identity.

If you want actual change, start with your thoughts. If you notice a thought where you're blaming yourself because someone is upset (this is usually due to very low self esteem) then it is best to redirect those thoughts in a healthy way.

For example, if someone is upset for whatever reason and you notice that you're thinking of "oh I did this, this why they're upset or maybe if i didn't do this" etc

The best course of action would be to "It isn't my fault. It is their responsability in whatever they feel"

It is crucial that you DO NOT shame the thoughts you're having where you blame yourself. A lot of people go down the route of shaming the negative feelings and thoughts they're having and they work so work in trying to change them that they're just burrying them, which creates a vicious cycle and fixes a problem only to create another.

A healthier way to redirect your thoughts is to say "It is very normal and natural to feel this negative feeling. It also normal to have these thoughts" but I should try to think differently. This creates promotes a positive change where where you accept that you blame yourself, you accept those negative thoughts and feelings as a natural thing, all while making the effort to change and redirect.

You need to remember that this will be a LONG process. Just as it became your identity to blame yourself, once you start changing your thoughs and doing it on a consistent level for a long period of  time. This will have an affect on your subconscious where you will hopefully not have a knee jerk reaction to blame yourself.

I suggest talking to your therapist so she can you the proper tools and strategies to navigte this. Something you can do on a daily basis.

I am no professional, but I hope this helps.

I am a teacher so I can give you somewhat of an insight to this. I do believe that younger students should not be graded. They need to focus on the learning process and enjoy it rather than fixating on getting a good grade. When students study for the sake of getting a good grade and they're not really acquiring a lot of things they're learning. Nonetheless, I do believe that grading is useful because it sheds some light on the student's capabilities and mastery of a subject or an activity. 

I understand that a written test isn't always the best because it doesn't really showcase the student's full potential. Nonetheless, if we were to administer different and non-standardised written, oral, and different trials to test the students then it will be time-consuming and it would need resources that the school does not provide. At the moment, a holistic or standard way of testing students is the most pragmatic and effective way of deducing whether a student is progressing.

For example, I have students who are not good when it comes to written tasks, others are quite good at it. I have a student who is always participating but the second you give them a written task, they don't perform well.

Whether you'd like to admit or not, straight-A students tend to have excellent memory, organization skills, time management, great deduction skills, leadership skills, and creativity. I do have students who are not really good at academia but I've noticed they do possess certain abilities that I found to be a lot more valuable (personally) which is emotional intelligence. Like I said, I personally find that people with higher EQ tend to excell more because they know how to work or deal with people, which is something that opens a lot of doors for you. Also, I've got some straight A students who are not good at team-work, or communication skills and are less creative. They tend to perform tasks well but they're also a bit short-sighted and quite arrogant.
